questions.q: Why does individual developer testing discipline tend to drift apart on a team without a written, shared standard?
options: Because Apex automatically randomizes test quality across developers
Because without a concrete, agreed checklist, code review relies on each reviewer independently remembering the same judgment calls, which doesn't stay consistent over time
Because Salesforce enforces different coverage rules for different developers
Drift doesn't actually happen in practice
questions.explain: Without a written standard, consistency depends on every reviewer independently applying the same judgment every time, which tends to drift as a team grows and people change — a concrete checklist gives review something specific to check against.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of CI enforcement (running tests and checking coverage automatically) compared to human code review?
options: CI enforcement cannot run Apex tests at all
CI can verify mechanical facts like pass/fail and coverage percentage, but it can't distinguish a meaningful assertion from a trivially-true one like System.assert(true)
CI enforcement always takes longer than manual testing
CI pipelines cannot be integrated with Salesforce at all
questions.explain: A CI pipeline enforces the mechanical gates (tests passed, coverage above threshold) reliably, but it has no way to judge whether an assertion is actually meaningful — that still requires human review of what the tests check.

options: A test that always fails, regardless of the code
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails against unchanged code
A test with no assertions at all
A test that only runs in sandbox orgs, never production
questions.explain: A flaky test is one that inconsistently passes or fails against code that hasn't changed, commonly caused by test order-dependence, shared/colliding test data, or an unreliable timing assumption.

questions.q: What is the recommended response to discovering a flaky test, per this lesson?
options: Re-run it repeatedly until it passes and move on without further investigation
Delete the test entirely so it stops reporting failures
Treat it like a bug report — investigate the cause (starting with test independence), and if it can't be fixed immediately, mark it clearly rather than silently tolerating it
Mark the whole test class as @isTest(SeeAllData=true) to stabilize it
questions.explain: Re-running until it passes just defers the same unreliable failure to the next person; the lesson recommends treating it as a real bug, investigating test independence first, and tracking it explicitly if it can't be fixed right away.

questions.q: Which of the following is suggested as part of a practical, test-focused pull request review checklist?
options: Whether the PR description states the before/after org-wide coverage number
Whether the developer personally feels confident about the code
Whether the test class uses exactly 10 test methods
Whether SeeAllData=true was used in every test class
questions.explain: The suggested checklist includes having the PR state its before/after org-wide coverage impact, alongside checks for positive/negative tests, bulk tests, mocked callouts, and absence of hardcoded Ids.
